megalosaurus:enwiki:21.title: Megalosaurus (Species named in the 20th century, part 2)

facts.statement: The genus Megalosaurus was first described by William Buckland in 1824.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Buckland, 1824

facts.statement: The type species of the genus is Megalosaurus bucklandii.
facts.quote: species: bucklandii

facts.statement: The species Megalosaurus bucklandii was named by Gideon Mantell in 1827.
facts.quote: authority: Mantell, 1827

facts.statement: Megalosaurus lived approximately 166 million years ago during the Middle Jurassic Bathonian age.
facts.quote: lived during the Middle Jurassic (Bathonian age, ~166 million years ago)

facts.statement: Megalosaurus fossils are found in what is now southern England.
facts.quote: in what is now southern England

facts.statement: William Buckland named the genus Megalosaurus in 1824.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus was named in 1824 by William Buckland

facts.statement: Gideon Mantell named the type species M. bucklandii in 1827 after William Buckland.
facts.quote: named in 1827 by Gideon Mantell, after Buckland

facts.statement: Richard Owen used Megalosaurus as one of the three genera to define the group Dinosauria in 1842.
facts.quote: In 1842, Megalosaurus was one of three genera on which Richard Owen based his Dinosauria

facts.statement: Megalosaurus was approximately 6 meters long and weighed about 700 kilograms.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus was about 6 m long, weighing about 700 kg

facts.statement: Megalosaurus was a bipedal dinosaur that walked on stout hindlimbs.
facts.quote: It was bipedal, walking on stout hindlimbs

facts.statement: Megalosaurus had short but very robust forelimbs.
facts.quote: Its forelimbs were short, though very robust

facts.statement: Megalosaurus had a large head equipped with long, curved teeth.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus had a rather large head, equipped with long curved teeth

facts.statement: Edward Lhuyd described a fossil tooth in 1699, which he believed to be from a fish.
facts.quote: In 1699, Edward Lhuyd described what he believed to have been a fish tooth

facts.statement: Specimen OU 1328 was lost and was not confidently assigned to Megalosaurus until it was re-described in 2002.
facts.quote: OU 1328 has since been lost and it was not confidently assigned to Megalosaurus until the tooth was re-described by Delair & Sarjeant (2002)

facts.statement: Specimen OU 1328 was collected near Witney, Oxfordshire during the 17th century.
facts.quote: OU 1328 was collected near Caswell, near Witney, Oxfordshire sometime during the 17th century

facts.statement: A fragment of a Megalosaurus bone was recovered from Stonesfield limestone quarry in Oxfordshire in 1676.
facts.quote: Part of a bone was recovered from the Taynton Limestone Formation of Stonesfield limestone quarry, Oxfordshire in 1676

facts.statement: Robert Plot published a description and illustration of the 1676 bone fragment in his Natural History of Oxfordshire in 1676.
facts.quote: Sir Thomas Pennyson gave the fragment to naturalist Robert Plot, who published a description and illustration in his Natural History of Oxfordshire in 1676

facts.statement: Robert Plot initially thought the bone belonged to a Roman war elephant and later to a giant human.
facts.quote: He therefore at first concluded it to be the thigh bone of a Roman war elephant and later that of a giant human

facts.statement: The ICZN Executive Secretary Philip K. Tubbs rejected a petition to suppress "Scrotum humanum" in favor of Megalosaurus.
facts.quote: However, the Executive Secretary of the ICZN at the time, Philip K. Tubbs, did not consider the petition to be admissible

facts.statement: The ICZN concluded that "Scrotum humanum" was not a valid scientific name because it was merely a label for an illustration.
facts.quote: concluding that the term "Scrotum humanum", published merely as a label for an illustration, did not constitute the valid creation of a new name

facts.statement: Today, only M. bucklandii is considered a true Megalosaurus species, as other species assigned to the genus are not directly related to it.
facts.quote: Today it is understood that none of these additional species was directly related to M. bucklandii, which is the only true Megalosaurus species

facts.statement: Much about Megalosaurus's build remains unclear because a complete skeleton has never been found.
facts.quote: Because a complete skeleton of it has never been found, much is still unclear about its build

facts.statement: A partial lower jaw of Megalosaurus was discovered about 40 feet underground in a Stonesfield Slate mine in the early 1790s.
facts.quote: It was discovered about 40 ft underground in a Stonesfield Slate mine during the early 1790s

facts.statement: The fossil layers containing Megalosaurus bones are part of the Taynton Limestone Formation, which dates to the mid-Bathonian stage of the Jurassic Period.
facts.quote: The layers there are currently considered part of the Taynton Limestone Formation, dating to the mid-Bathonian stage of the Jurassic Period

facts.statement: Megalosaurus was the first non-avian dinosaur genus to be named.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus was the first non-avian dinosaur genus named

facts.statement: In 1990, Ralph Molnar selected the dentary (front part of the lower jaw), specimen OUM J13505, as the lectotype for Megalosaurus.
facts.quote: In 1990, Ralph Molnar chose the famous dentary (front part of the lower jaw), OUM J13505, as such a lectotype

facts.statement: William Buckland classified Megalosaurus as a giant animal belonging to the Sauria, a group of lizards that at the time included crocodiles.
facts.quote: Buckland identified the organism as being a giant animal belonging to the Sauria – the Lizards, at the time seen as including the crocodiles

facts.statement: William Buckland and William Conybeare intended to name two gigantic lizard-like creatures in a joint article included in Cuvier's Ossemens.
facts.quote: Buckland and Conybeare, in a joint article to be included in Cuvier's Ossemens, intended to provide scientific names for both gigantic lizard-like creatures known at the time

facts.statement: William Conybeare devised the name Megalosaurus, derived from the Greek word for 'large'.
facts.quote: Conybeare had devised the name "Megalosaurus", from the Greek μέγας, megas, "large"

facts.statement: Although a planned publication failed in 1822, the physician James Parkinson announced the name Megalosaurus that same year.
facts.quote: That year a publication failed to occur, but the physician James Parkinson already in 1822 announced the name "Megalosaurus"

facts.statement: The descriptions of Megalosaurus bones published in the Transactions of the Geological Society in 1824 constituted a valid publication of the name.
facts.quote: The descriptions of the bones in the Transactions of the Geological Society, in 1824, constitute a valid publication of the name

facts.statement: Because the original fossils represented several individuals, they formed a syntype series rather than a single type specimen.
facts.quote: Because they represented several individuals, the described fossils formed a syntype series

facts.statement: Among the original fossils collected by Buckland, only the sacrum was articulated.
facts.quote: only the sacrum was articulated

facts.statement: Mary Morland provided drawings of the bones that served as the basis for illustrating lithographies.
facts.quote: Mary provided drawings of the bones, that were to be the basis of illustrating lithographies

facts.statement: Buckland originally described Megalosaurus as a quadruped.
facts.quote: He considered Megalosaurus to be a quadruped.

facts.statement: Buckland imagined Megalosaurus to resemble a gigantic lizard.
facts.quote: Generally, in his mind Megalosaurus resembled a gigantic lizard

facts.statement: Buckland noted that the thigh bone shape suggested Megalosaurus held its legs upright rather than sprawling.
facts.quote: Buckland already understood from the form of the thigh bone head that the legs were not so much sprawling as held rather upright.

facts.statement: Buckland's 1824 description estimated Megalosaurus at 40 feet long and weighing as much as a seven-foot-tall elephant.
facts.quote: In the original description of 1824, Buckland repeated Cuvier's size estimate that Megalosaurus would have been 40 feet long with the weight of a seven foot tall elephant.

facts.statement: Buckland was hurried into naming Megalosaurus after visiting Mantell's fossil collection.
facts.quote: Buckland had also been hurried into naming his new reptile by a visit he had made to the fossil collection of Mantell

facts.statement: Mantell announced he had found a fossil thigh bone twice as long as the one previously described.
facts.quote: Mantell, who during the lecture announced to have acquired a fossil thigh bone of enormous magnitude, twice as long as that just described.

facts.statement: The large thigh bone Mantell found was later identified as belonging to Iguanodon, though Buckland and Mantell initially thought it belonged to Megalosaurus.
facts.quote: Today, this is known to have belonged to Iguanodon, or at least some iguanodontid, but at the time both men assumed this bone belonged to Megalosaurus also.

facts.statement: The existence of Megalosaurus challenged Christian orthodoxy regarding the origin of suffering and death.
facts.quote: The existence of Megalosaurus posed some problems for Christian orthodoxy, which typically held that suffering and death had only come into the world through Original Sin

facts.statement: Richard Owen claimed on 2 August 1841 that certain prehistoric reptiles had reached the organizational level of mammals.
facts.quote: In reaction, on 2 August 1841 Richard Owen during a lecture to the British Association for the Advancement of Science claimed that certain prehistoric reptilian groups had already attained the organisational level of present mammals

facts.statement: Owen listed Megalosaurus as one of three examples of higher-level reptiles alongside Iguanodon and Hylaeosaurus.
facts.quote: Owen presented three examples of such higher level reptiles: Iguanodon, Hylaeosaurus and Megalosaurus.

facts.statement: Owen calculated a total body length of 30 feet for Megalosaurus by adding known vertebrae lengths.
facts.quote: By simply adding the known length of the vertebrae, instead of extrapolating from a lizard, Owen arrived at a total body length for Megalosaurus of 30 feet.

facts.statement: Owen united Megalosaurus, Iguanodon, and Hylaeosaurus into the group Dinosauria in 1842.
facts.quote: In the printed version of the lecture published in 1842, Owen united the three reptiles into a separate group: the Dinosauria.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus was one of the three original dinosaurs defined by Owen.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus was thus one of the three original dinosaurs.

facts.statement: A life-sized concrete model of Megalosaurus built by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins in 1852 remains at Crystal Palace Park.
facts.quote: In 1852, Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins was commissioned to build a life-sized concrete model of Megalosaurus for the exhibition of prehistoric animals at the Crystal Palace Park in Sydenham, where it remains to this day.

facts.statement: The Crystal Palace model of Megalosaurus features a shoulder hump, possibly inspired by vertebral spines Owen acquired in the early 1850s.
facts.quote: The sculpture in Crystal Palace Park shows a conspicuous hump on the shoulders and it has been suggested this was inspired by a set of high vertebral spines acquired by Owen in the early 1850s.

facts.statement: Owen referred high vertebral spines to Megalosaurus, though they are now classified as the separate genus Becklespinax.
facts.quote: Today, they are seen as a separate genus Becklespinax, but Owen referred them to Megalosaurus.

facts.statement: The Crystal Palace exhibition created public awareness in England that ancient reptiles existed.
facts.quote: The models at the exhibition created a general public awareness for the first time, at least in England, that ancient reptiles had existed.

facts.statement: The Oxford University Museum of Natural History display includes most specimens from Buckland's original Megalosaurus description.
facts.quote: The Oxford University Museum of Natural History display contains most of the specimens from the original description by Buckland.

facts.statement: Stonesfield quarries worked until 1911 produced mostly single pelvis and hindlimb bones of Megalosaurus bucklandii.
facts.quote: The quarries at Stonesfield, which were worked until 1911, continued to produce Megalosaurus bucklandii fossils, mostly single bones from the pelvis and hindlimbs.

facts.statement: Roger Benson counted 103 specimens from the Stonesfield Slate representing a minimum of seven individuals in 2010.
facts.quote: In 2010, Roger Benson counted a total of 103 specimens from the Stonesfield Slate, from a minimum of seven individuals.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Stonesfield material represents a single taxon.
facts.quote: It has been contentious whether this material represents just a single taxon.

facts.statement: Day and Barrett claimed two morphotypes of Megalosaurus existed based on thighbone differences in 2004.
facts.quote: In 2004, Julia Day and Paul Barrett claimed that there were two morphotypes present, based on small differences in the thighbones.

facts.statement: Benson initially favored the two-morphotype idea in 2008 but concluded the differences were illusory in 2010.
facts.quote: In 2008 Benson favoured this idea, but in 2010 concluded the differences were illusory.

facts.statement: Thomas Huxley assigned maxilla fragment OUM J13506 to M. bucklandii in 1869.
facts.quote: A maxilla fragment, specimen OUM J13506, was, in 1869 assigned, by Thomas Huxley, to M. bucklandii.

facts.statement: Benson found the maxilla fragment indistinguishable from other M. bucklandii maxillae in 2010.
facts.quote: In 2010, Benson pointed out that the fragment was basically indistinguishable from other known M. bucklandii maxillae, to which it had in fact not been compared by the other authors.

facts.statement: Remains from the early Bathonian Chipping Norton Limestone Formation were referred to Megalosaurus in 1939.
facts.quote: Apart from the finds in the Taynton Limestone Formation, in 1939 Sidney Hugh Reynolds referred remains to Megalosaurus that had been found in the older Chipping Norton Limestone Formation dating from the early Bathonian, about 30 single teeth and bones.

facts.statement: Benson affirmed the reference of New Park Quarry remains to M. bucklandii in 2009 despite age disparities.
facts.quote: Though the age disparity makes it problematic to assume an identity with Megalosaurus bucklandii, in 2009 Benson could not establish any relevant anatomical differences with M. bucklandii among the remains found at one site, the New Park Quarry, and therefore affirmed the reference to that species.

facts.statement: An ilium from Oakham Quarry was clearly dissimilar to M. bucklandii.
facts.quote: However, in another site, the Oakham Quarry, the material contained one bone, an ilium, that was clearly dissimilar.

facts.statement: Trace fossils have sometimes been referred to Megalosaurus or the ichnogenus Megalosauripus.
facts.quote: Sometimes trace fossils have been referred to Megalosaurus or to the ichnogenus Megalosauripus.

facts.statement: Fossilized footprints were found at Ardley in 1997, 20 kilometers northeast of Oxford.
facts.quote: In 1997, a famous group of fossilized footprints (ichnites) was found in a limestone quarry at Ardley, 20 kilometers northeast of Oxford.

facts.statement: The Ardley footprints were thought to be made by Megalosaurus and possibly Cetiosaurus.
facts.quote: They were thought to have been made by Megalosaurus and possibly also some left by Cetiosaurus.

facts.statement: Replicas of the Ardley footprints are displayed on the lawn of the Oxford University Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: There are replicas of some of these footprints, set across the lawn of the Oxford University Museum of Natural History.

facts.statement: One of the Ardley tracks shows a theropod accelerating from walking to running.
facts.quote: One track was of a theropod accelerating from walking to running.

facts.statement: Benson argues that track referrals to Megalosaurus are unprovable due to lack of unique traits.
facts.quote: According to Benson, such referrals are unprovable, as the tracks show no traits unique to Megalosaurus.

facts.statement: No complete skeleton of Megalosaurus has been found despite many bone discoveries.
facts.quote: Since the first finds, many other Megalosaurus bones have been recovered; however, no complete skeleton has yet been found.

facts.statement: The details of Megalosaurus's physical appearance remain uncertain due to the lack of a complete skeleton.
facts.quote: Therefore, the details of its physical appearance cannot be certain.

facts.statement: A full osteology of all known Megalosaurus material was published by Benson in 2010.
facts.quote: However, a full osteology of all known material was published in 2010 by Benson.

facts.statement: In 1984, David Bruce Norman estimated that Megalosaurus was between seven and eight meters long.
facts.quote: David Bruce Norman in 1984 thought Megalosaurus was seven to eight meters long.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul tentatively estimated Megalosaurus weighed 1.1 tons in 1988, based on a thigh bone measuring 76 centimeters.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul in 1988 estimated the weight tentatively at 1.1 tons, given a thigh bone 76 centimeters long.

facts.statement: In 2010, Gregory S. Paul revised his estimates to suggest Megalosaurus was 6 meters long and weighed 700 kilograms.
facts.quote: Paul in 2010 estimated the size of Megalosaurus at 6 m in length and 700 kg.

facts.statement: A thigh bone 803 millimeters long found in specimen NHMUK PV OR 31806 suggests a body weight of 943 kilograms when using J.F. Anderson's extrapolation method.
facts.quote: Specimen NHMUK PV OR 31806, a thigh bone 803 millimeters long, would indicate a body weight of 943 kilograms, using the extrapolation method of J.F. Anderson

facts.statement: Megalosaurus had long, strong hindlimbs with three forward-facing toes and short, robust forelimbs that likely carried three digits.
facts.quote: The hindlimbs were long and strong with three forward-facing weight-bearing toes, the forelimbs relatively short but exceptionally robust and probably carrying three digits.

facts.statement: As a carnivore, Megalosaurus possessed a large, elongated head with long, dagger-like teeth designed to slice prey flesh.
facts.quote: Being a carnivore, its large elongated head bore long dagger-like teeth to slice the flesh of its prey.

facts.statement: The maxilla of Megalosaurus bears 13 teeth.
facts.quote: The maxilla bears 13 teeth.

facts.statement: The teeth of Megalosaurus are relatively large, with a crown length reaching up to seven centimeters.
facts.quote: The teeth are relatively large, with a crown length up to seven centimeters.

facts.statement: The cutting edges of Megalosaurus teeth bear between 18 and 20 denticula per centimeter.
facts.quote: The cutting edges bear 18 to 20 denticula per centimeter.

facts.statement: The high level of pneumatization in the jugal bone of Megalosaurus is unique among megalosaurids and may represent a separate autapomorphy.
facts.quote: Such a level of pneumatisation of the jugal is not known from other megalosaurids and might represent a separate autapomorphy.

facts.statement: A broken cervical vertebra from the New Park Quarry reveals large internal air chambers and heavy pneumatization with large pleurocoels on its sides.
facts.quote: The breakage reveals large internal air chambers. The vertebra is also otherwise heavily pneumatized, with large pleurocoels, pneumatic excavations, on its sides.

facts.statement: The only known ulna specimen of Megalosaurus is 232 millimeters long with a minimal shaft circumference of 142 millimeters.
facts.quote: The only known specimen, NHMUK PV OR 36585, has a length of 232 millimeters and a minimal shaft circumference of 142 millimeters.

facts.statement: The ulna of Megalosaurus is more heavily built than that of any other known Tetanurae dinosaur.
facts.quote: The ulna is extremely robust, for its absolute size more heavily built than with any other known member of the Tetanurae.

facts.statement: The third metatarsal of Megalosaurus lacks clear condyles, creating a flexible joint capable of horizontal movement.
facts.quote: The third metatarsal has no clear condyles at its lower end, resulting in a more flexible joint, allowing for a modicum of horizontal movement.

facts.statement: A unique ridge on the third metatarsal fits into a groove on the second metatarsal to create a tighter connection between the bones.
facts.quote: The top inner side of the third metatarsal carries a unique ridge that fits into a groove along the top outer side of the second metatarsal, causing a tighter connection.

facts.statement: Thick bony skirts between the ischial shafts touch to form an almost flat surface in Megalosaurus.
facts.quote: The bony skirts between the shafts of the ischia are thick and touch each other forming an almost flat surface.

facts.statement: The underside of the second sacral vertebra possesses an angular longitudinal keel.
facts.quote: The underside of the second sacral vertebra has an angular longitudinal keel.

facts.statement: For decades after its discovery, researchers considered Megalosaurus the definitive or typical large carnivorous dinosaur.
facts.quote: For decades after its discovery, Megalosaurus was seen by researchers as the definitive or typical large carnivorous dinosaur.

facts.statement: During the 20th century, the genus Megalosaurus was commonly restricted to fossils found in the Middle Jurassic of England.
facts.quote: This slowly changed during the 20th century, when it became common to restrict the genus to fossils found in the middle Jurassic of England.

facts.statement: A 2008 study by Roger Benson and colleagues identified unique characteristics in the lower jaw that separated Megalosaurus from other megalosaurids.
facts.quote: However, a comprehensive study by Roger Benson and colleagues in 2008, and several related analyses published in subsequent years, overturned the previous consensus by identifying several autapomorphies, or unique distinguishing characteristics, in the lower jaw that could be used to separate Megalosaurus from other megalosaurids.

facts.statement: Roger Benson concluded that the Stonesfield Slate material likely represents a single species.
facts.quote: Benson also concluded it would be most parsimonious to assume that the Stonesfield Slate material represents a single species.

facts.statement: Richard Owen placed Megalosaurus as one of the first three genera in the Dinosauria in 1842.
facts.quote: In 1842, Owen made Megalosaurus one of the first three genera placed in the Dinosauria.

facts.statement: Prince Charles Lucien Bonaparte coined the family Megalosauridae with Megalosaurus as the type genus in 1850.
facts.quote: In 1850, Prince Charles Lucien Bonaparte coined a separate family Megalosauridae with Megalosaurus as the type genus.

facts.statement: A 2012 study by Matthew Carrano et al. identified Megalosaurus as the sister species of Torvosaurus within the Megalosaurinae.
facts.quote: In 2012, Matthew Carrano et al. showed that Megalosaurus was the sister species of Torvosaurus within the Megalosaurinae, giving this cladogram:

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the Stonesfield Slate fossils, associated with Megalosaurus, may belong to several possibly unrelated theropod species.
facts.quote: Further restriction occurred in the late 20th and early 21st centuries, researchers such as Ronan Allain and Dan Chure suggesting that the Stonesfield Slate fossils perhaps belonged to several, possibly not directly related, species of theropod dinosaur.

facts.statement: Some researchers argue that Megalosaurus is a nomen dubium because they could not find characteristics to distinguish it from its relatives.
facts.quote: Furthermore, several researchers failed to find any characteristics in that jaw that could be used to distinguish Megalosaurus from its relatives, which would mean the genus were a nomen dubium.

facts.statement: A 2008 study overturned the consensus that Megalosaurus was a nomen dubium by identifying unique characteristics in the lower jaw.
facts.quote: However, a comprehensive study by Roger Benson and colleagues in 2008, and several related analyses published in subsequent years, overturned the previous consensus by identifying several autapomorphies, or unique distinguishing characteristics, in the lower jaw that could be used to separate Megalosaurus from other megalosaurids.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus lived in Europe during the Middle Jurassic, approximately 166 to 168 million years ago.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus lived in what is now Europe during the Bathonian stage of the Middle Jurassic (~166-168 million years ago).

facts.statement: Researcher Benson concluded in 2010 that Megalosaurus was the apex predator of its habitat based on its size and distribution.
facts.quote: Benson in 2010 concluded from its size and common distribution that Megalosaurus was the apex predator of its habitat.

facts.statement: Scientists question why Megalosaurus did not exhibit insular dwarfism despite living on an island landmass comparable in size to Cuba.
facts.quote: It has been questioned why the dinosaurs of the island did not experience insular dwarfism, as would be expected for an island of this size.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus may have hunted stegosaurs and sauropods.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus may have hunted stegosaurs and sauropods.

facts.statement: In 1857, Joseph Leidy renamed Deinodon horridus to Megalosaurus horridus, a name meaning "the frightening one" based on teeth.
facts.quote: In 1857, Joseph Leidy renamed Deinodon horridus (Leidy, 1856) into Megalosaurus horridus, the "frightening one", a genus based on teeth.

facts.statement: In 1870, Jean-Baptiste Greppin named Megalosaurus meriani based on a premaxillary tooth found near Moutier.
facts.quote: In 1870, Jean-Baptiste Greppin named Megalosaurus meriani based on specimen MH 350, a premaxillary tooth found near Moutier and part of the collection of Peter Merian.

facts.statement: In 1871, Emanuel Bunzel named Megalosaurus schnaitheimi based on remains found near Schnaitheim.
facts.quote: In 1871, Emanuel Bunzel named remains found near Schnaitheim Megalosaurus schnaitheimi.

facts.statement: In 1876, J. Henry named Megalosaurus obtusus, meaning "the blunt one", based on four Late Triassic teeth found near Moissey.
facts.quote: In 1876, J. Henry, a science teacher at Besançon, in a published dissertation named four Late Triassic possible dinosaur teeth found near Moissey Megalosaurus obtusus, "the blunt one".

facts.statement: In 1881, Harry Govier Seeley named Megalosaurus pannoniensis based on two possible theropod teeth found in Austria, a name referring to Pannonia.
facts.quote: In 1881, Harry Govier Seeley named two possible theropod teeth found in Austria Megalosaurus pannoniensis. The specific name refers to Pannonia.

facts.statement: In 1882, Henri-Émile Sauvage named Megalosaurus superbus, meaning "the proud one", based on Early Cretaceous teeth and vertebrae found at Louppy-le-Château.
facts.quote: In 1882, Henri-Émile Sauvage named remains found at Louppy-le-Château, teeth and vertebrae from the Early Cretaceous, Megalosaurus superbus, "the proud one".

facts.statement: In 1884/1885, Wilhelm Barnim Dames named Megalosaurus dunkeri based on an Early Cretaceous tooth honoring Wilhelm Dunker.
facts.quote: In 1884/1885, Wilhelm Barnim Dames, based on specimen UM 84, a tooth from the Early Cretaceous, named Megalosaurus dunkeri, the specific name honouring Wilhelm Dunker.

facts.statement: In 1889, Richard Lydekker named Megalosaurus oweni based on Early Cretaceous metatarsals honoring Owen.
facts.quote: In 1889, Richard Lydekker named Megalosaurus oweni, the specific name honouring Owen, based on a series of metatarsals from the Early Cretaceous, specimen BMNH R?2556?.

facts.statement: In 1892, Edward Drinker Cope renamed Ceratosaurus nasicornis to Megalosaurus nasicornis.
facts.quote: In 1892, Edward Drinker Cope renamed Ceratosaurus nasicornis Marsh 1884 into Megalosaurus nasicornis.

facts.statement: In 1896, Charles Jean Julien Depéret named Megalosaurus crenatissimus, meaning "the much crenelated", based on Late Cretaceous remains found in Madagascar.
facts.quote: In 1896, Charles Jean Julien Depéret named Megalosaurus crenatissimus, "the much crenelated", based on remains from the Late Cretaceous found in Madagascar.

facts.statement: In 1898, Henry Fairfield Osborn renamed Laelaps aquilunguis to Megalosaurus aquilunguis.
facts.quote: Henry Fairfield Osborn, a partisan of Cope, rejected this replacement and thus in 1898 renamed Laelaps aquilunguis Cope 1866 into Megalosaurus aquilunguis.

facts.statement: In 1901, Baron Franz Nopcsa renamed the species Laelaps trihedrodon to Megalosaurus trihedrodon.
facts.quote: In 1901 Baron Franz Nopcsa renamed Laelaps trihedrodon Cope 1877 into Megalosaurus trihedrodon.

facts.statement: In 1910, Arthur Smith Woodward named Megalosaurus bradleyi based on a Middle Jurassic skull, honoring collector F. Lewis Bradley.
facts.quote: In 1910, Arthur Smith Woodward named Megalosaurus bradleyi based on a skull from the Middle Jurassic, the specific name honouring the collector F. Lewis Bradley.

facts.statement: In 1925, Depéret named Megalosaurus saharicus based on two teeth found in Algeria.
facts.quote: In 1925, Depéret, based on two teeth from Algeria, named Megalosaurus saharicus.

facts.statement: In 1954, Samuel Welles named Megalosaurus wetherilli based on a nearly complete Early Jurassic skeleton found in Arizona.
facts.quote: In 1954 Samuel Welles named Megalosaurus wetherilli. This species is exceptional in being based on a rather complete skeleton, found in Arizona, from the Early Jurassic.

facts.statement: In 1955, Albert-Félix de Lapparent named Megalosaurus mersensis based on 23 vertebrae found in the El Mers Formation of Morocco.
facts.quote: In 1955, Albert-Félix de Lapparent named Megalosaurus mersensis based on a series of 23 vertebrae found near Tizi n'Juillerh in a layer of the El Mers Formation of Morocco.

facts.statement: In 1970, Rodney Steel renamed two species into Megalosaurus: Iliosuchus incognitus and Nuthetes destructor.
facts.quote: In 1970, Rodney Steel named two Megalosaurus species. Firstly, he renamed Iliosuchus incognitus Huene 1932 into Megalosaurus incognitus. Secondly, he renamed Nuthetes destructor Owen 1854 into Megalosaurus destructor.

facts.statement: In 2025, Megalosaurus cambrensis was formally re-described as Newtonsaurus cambrensis, identified as a primitive theropod outside Averostra.
facts.quote: In 2025, it was formally described as Newtonsaurus cambrensis, in a study that demonstrated unambiguously that it was a relatively primitive theropod dinosaur, a possibly coelophysoid member of Neotheropoda outside of Averostra.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Megalosaurus valens likely represents fossil material of Allosaurus.
facts.quote: In the same publication Nopcsa renamed Poekilopleuron valens Leidy 1870 into Megalosaurus valens; this probably represents fossil material of Allosaurus.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Megalosaurus lonzeensis represents a Noasaurid or an indeterminate Coelurosaurian.
facts.quote: It perhaps represents a member of the Noasauridae, or an indeterminate member of the Coelurosauria.

facts.statement: There is a debate over whether Megalosaurus ingens represents a large Carcharodontosaurid or an indeterminate Tetanuran.
facts.quote: It possibly represents a large member of the Carcharodontosauridae; Carrano e.a. saw it as an indeterminate member of the Tetanurae.

facts.statement: Current opinion suggests Megalosaurus mersensis likely represents a member of the Mesosuchia (crocodilians).
facts.quote: This probably represents a member of the Mesosuchia.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus inexpectatus might represent a member of the Carcharodontosauridae.
facts.quote: It might represent a member of the Carcharodontosauridae.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus schmidti is considered a chimaera, combining parts of different species.
facts.quote: It is a chimaera.

facts.statement: It is suggested that Megalosaurus cambrensis probably represents a member of the Coelophysoidea or another predatory archosaur.

facts.statement: A 2012 study by Carrano, Benson, and Sampson analyzed the phylogeny of Tetanurae, the group containing Megalosaurus.

facts.statement: The species Megalosaurus bucklandii was named by Gideon Mantell in 1827 in honor of William Buckland.
facts.quote: La especie, dedicada a Buckland, fue nombrada por Gideon Mantell en 1827.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus was a bipedal predator approximately 9 meters long and weighing around one tonne, with a body structure balanced for running.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus fue un depredador bípedo de unos 9 metros de largo y alrededor de una tonelada de peso con una estructura bien balanceada para la carrera.

facts.statement: Like other theropods, Megalosaurus had three toes on the front foot and one inverted toe.
facts.quote: Como todos los terópodos, tenía tres dedos en la parte delantera del pie y uno solo invertido.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus lived in the middle Jurassic period, approximately 166 million years ago during the Bathonian stage, in what is now Europe.
facts.quote: que vivió a mediados del período Jurásico, hace aproximadamente 166 millones de años, en el Bathoniense, en lo que hoy es Europa.

facts.statement: Living in what is now Europe during the Jurassic period between 181 and 169 million years ago, Megalosaurus may have hunted stegosaurs and sauropods.
facts.quote: Viviendo en lo que ahora es Europa, durante el período Jurásico, hace 181 a 169 millones de años, Megalosaurus pudo haber cazado estegosauros y saurópodos.

facts.statement: Although Megalosaurus was a large carnivore capable of attacking large sauropods, it likely obtained some food through scavenging.
facts.quote: Aunque Megalosaurus era un carnívoro grande y habría podido atacar probablemente incluso los saurópodos más grandes, es también probable que consiguiera algo de su alimento por el carroñeo.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus had small forelimbs with probable digits, though not as tiny as in modern theropods like Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: Aunque no habían alcanzado el tamaño minúsculo como en otros terópodos más modernos como el Tyrannosaurus, los miembros delanteros de Megalosaurus eran pequeños y tenían probablemente dígitos.

facts.statement: Many Megalosaurus bones have been recovered since the initial findings, but a complete skeleton has not yet been found.
facts.quote: Desde los primeros hallazgos, se han recuperado muchos otros huesos de Megalosaurus, sin embargo, aún no se ha encontrado un esqueleto completo.

facts.statement: Traditionally, most texts following Owen's 1841 estimate state that Megalosaurus had a body length of 9 meters.
facts.quote: Tradicionalmente, la mayoría de los textos, siguiendo la estimación de Owen de 1841, dan una longitud corporal de 9 metros para Megalosaurus.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul tentatively estimated Megalosaurus weighed 1.1 tonnes based on a femur length of 76 centimeters in 1988.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul en 1988 estimó el peso tentativamente en 1,1 toneladas, dado un fémur de 76 centímetros de largo.

facts.statement: In 2010, Paul stated that Megalosaurus measured 6 meters in length and weighed 700 kilograms.
facts.quote: Paul en 2010 declaró Megalosaurus medía 6 metros de largo y 700 kilogramos de peso.

facts.statement: The thigh bone specimen OUM J13561 has a length of approximately 86 centimeters.
facts.quote: Además, el espécimen de hueso del muslo OUM J13561 tiene una longitud de aproximadamente 86 centímetros.

facts.statement: The upper jaw of Megalosaurus has 13 teeth.
facts.quote: El maxilar tiene 13 dientes.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus teeth were relatively large, with a crown length of up to 7 centimeters.
facts.quote: Los dientes son relativamente grandes, con una longitud de corona de hasta 7 centímetros.

facts.statement: The cutting edges of Megalosaurus teeth have between 18 and 20 denticles per centimeter.
facts.quote: Los bordes cortantes tienen entre 18 y 20 denticulos por centímetro.

facts.statement: The jugal bone in Megalosaurus is pneumaticized, perforated by a large hole from the direction of the antorbital fenestra.
facts.quote: El hueso yugal está neumatizado, perforado por un gran agujero desde la dirección de la fenestra antorbital.

facts.statement: This level of jugal pneumatization is unknown in other megalosauroids and could represent a separate autapomorphy.
facts.quote: Tal nivel de neumatización del yugal no se conoce de otros megalosáuridos y podría representar una autapomorfia separada.

facts.statement: The number of lower jaw teeth was probably thirteen or fourteen, though damaged preserved samples show a maximum of eleven alveoli.
facts.quote: El número de dientes dentales probablemente fue de trece o catorce, aunque las muestras dañadas conservadas muestran como máximo once alvéolos.

facts.statement: At one time, Megalosaurus was a "wastebasket taxon" used to classify many types of large theropods.
facts.quote: En un tiempo, Megalosaurus fue un "taxón cajón de sastre", usado para clasificar muchas clases de grandes terópodos.

facts.statement: In recent years, the genus has undergone extensive reconsideration, and most species have been removed from it.
facts.quote: En los años recientes, el género ha estado sujeto a una extensa reconsideración y la mayor parte de las especies han sido eliminadas del mismo.

facts.statement: Repeated descriptions of Megalosaurus hunting iguanodontes are likely inaccurate because iguanodont skeletons are found in Lower Cretaceous formations, much younger than the Middle Jurassic formations where megalosaurians originate.
facts.quote: Las descripciones repetidas de la caza de iguanodontes por el megalosaurio a través de los bosques que entonces cubrieron el continente son probablemente inexactas, porque los esqueletos de iguanodonte se encuentran en formaciones del Cretácico Inferior, mucho más jóvenes que las del Jurásico Medio de donde provienen los megalosaurios.

facts.statement: Several traits identified in 2008 as autapomorphies were later discovered to be the result of damage.
facts.quote: Varios rasgos identificados en 2008 como autapomorfias, que luego se descubrieron como resultado de daños.

facts.statement: The vertebral column of Megalosaurus likely consisted of ten cervical, thirteen dorsal, five sacral, and fifty to sixty caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: Aunque se desconocen los números exactos, la columna vertebral de Megalosaurus probablemente se dividió en diez vértebras del cuello, trece vértebras dorsales, cinco vértebras sacras y cincuenta a sesenta vértebras de la cola

facts.statement: A broken cervical vertebra reveals large internal air chambers and is highly pneumatic with large pleurocoels on the sides.
facts.quote: La rotura revela grandes cámaras de aire internas. La vértebra también es muy neumática, con grandes pleurocelos, excavaciones neumáticas, a los lados.

facts.statement: The neural spines at the base of the tail are transversely thin and tall.
facts.quote: Las espinas neurales de la base de la cola son transversalmente delgadas y altas.

facts.statement: In 1852, Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins was commissioned to build a Megalosaurus model for the Crystal Palace exhibition, which is still preserved today.
facts.quote: En 1852, Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins fue comisionado para construir un modelo de Megalosaurus para la exhibición del Crystal Palace, que se conserva aún hoy en día.

facts.statement: Early paleontologists reconstructed Megalosaurus as a four-legged dragon with a huge head based on popular mythology before seeing the creature.
facts.quote: Los primeros paleontólogos, nunca habían visto una criatura como esta anteriormente, reconstruyéndolos como dragón en la mitología popular, con una enorme cabeza y caminando sobre cuatro patas.

facts.statement: Friedrich von Huene's drawing of Megalosaurus used dorsal spines from Altispinax, a large theropod known for high dorsal spines and occasionally classified as a spinosaurid.
facts.quote: Mientras que el dibujo de Friedrich von Huene de la Universidad de Tübingen, Alemania, utilizó las espinas dorsales de Altispinax, un misterioso terópodo grande conocido por las altas espinas de sus vértebras dorsales y clasificado ocasionalmente como espinosáurido.

facts.statement: In 1956, Von Huene found remains he called Megalosaurus africanus in Cretaceous sediments, which were later classified as Carcharodontosaurus.
facts.quote: En 1956 Von Huene encontró restos de lo que llamó Megalosaurus africanus en sedimentos del Cretácico que luego fueron clasificado como Carcharodontosaurus.

facts.statement: In 1995, a tibia with three robust metatarsi led to the proposal of a second species, M. phillipsi, which is now doubtful.
facts.quote: En 1995 el hallazgo de una tibia con tres metatarsos, que eran más gruesos y fuertes que lo del M. bucklandii llevó a proponer una segunda especie llamada M. phillipsi que se encuentra en duda.

facts.statement: In 2010, Roger Benson counted a total of 103 specimens from the Stonesfield Slate, representing a minimum of seven individuals.
facts.quote: En 2010, Roger Benson contó un total de 103 especímenes de la pizarra de Stonesfield, de un mínimo de siete individuos.

facts.statement: It is debated whether two morphotypes exist in the Stonesfield material; while Day and Barrett (2004) and Benson (2008) suggested differences in femur bones, Benson (2010) concluded these differences were illusory.
facts.quote: En 2004, Julia Day y Paul Barrett afirmaron que había dos morfotipos presentes, basados en pequeñas diferencias en los huesos del muslo. En 2008 Benson favoreció esta idea, pero en 2010 concluyó que las diferencias eran ilusorias.

facts.statement: The classification of a specific jaw fragment is debated, with Bakker (1992) suggesting Sinraptoridae and Naish (2007) suggesting Abelisauroidea.
facts.quote: En 1992 Robert Thomas Bakker afirmó que representaba a un miembro de los Sinraptoridae en 2007, Darren Naish pensó que era una especie separada perteneciente a los Abelisauroidea.

facts.statement: It is debated whether trackways found in Ardley Quarry were made by Megalosaurus; while some show a theropod accelerating from walking to running, Benson notes they lack exclusive Megalosaurus traits.
facts.quote: A veces, los fósiles de huellas se han referido a Megalosaurus o al icnogénero Megalosauripus. En 1997, se encontró un famoso grupo de huellas fosilizadas, icnitas, en una cantera de piedra caliza en Ardley, a veinte kilómetros al noreste de Oxford. Se pensaba que habían sido hechos por Megalosaurus y posiblemente también algunos dejados por Cetiosaurus. Hay réplicas de algunas de estas huellas, ubicadas en el césped del Museo de Historia Natural de la Universidad de Oxford. Una huella era de un terópodo acelerando de caminar a correr. Según Benson, tales referencias no son demostrables, ya que las huellas no muestran rasgos exclusivos de Megalosaurus.

facts.statement: A Megalosaurus rib described by Sir Richard Owen shows a pathological swelling caused by a healed fracture at the point where it would have articulated with its vertebra.
facts.quote: Una costilla de Megalosaurus descrita en 1856 y 1884 por Sir Richard Owen tiene una mancha inflamada patológica cerca de la base de su proceso capitular. El punto hinchado parece haber sido causado por una fractura curada y se encuentra en el punto donde se habría articulado con su vértebra.
